cards.title: I Love Software Rendering

depth.text: someone loves running old DOS games with software rendering for their **sharp, gritty look**

The author wants the original DOS versions on **real hardware**, rather than in DOSBox; Windows source ports are another option. Quake runs at **800×600** and a locked **60fps** on a Dell OptiPlex 380, while Tomb Raider’s underwater sections look better accelerated.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say the appeal is pixelated textures or turning off anti-aliasing, not software rendering; others defend software rendering as a distinct way to draw games.

comments.text: This isn't software rendering, it's called turning off spatial anti-aliasing. You can still do that in the modernest of modern games. Software rendering went out of the window because the CPU tends to have other things to do whilst playing the game besides only multiplying 4x4 matrices, which was shifted to the shader cores of GPUs. The look-and-feel that the author is discussing including shadow…
This should really be titled "I love pixelated textures". > " 3D cards smoothed textures with bilinear filtering " You can just not do that.
Ah the software rendering era. Where I gained 10fps by adding a sound card.

Everyone is already pointing out this isn't quite software rendering but rather the rendering technique which used to be the only option. I'll add that even without a GPU, CPUs will have integrated graphics. There are CPUs that don't have this but in those cases you need a GPU. The point is that modern systems no longer use CPU to output to the screen, either there is an integrated GPU or a GPU…

Software rendering often provided better visual effects than the GPU paths could provide at the time. A general purpose CPU can technically do any effect since the software is the pixel shader. Programmable shader pipelines weren't a thing until Geforce 3 in 2001.

cards.title: The Folders Programming Language

depth.text: someone made a programming language where **folder structure** does the work of **code**
Folder names are ignored apart from **alphabetical ordering**; the number of subfolders in a command’s first folder determines its **type**. Temp folders store data in their **names**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some love the weird idea; others call it pointless or say filesystem metadata still takes space.

comments.text: "In Windows, folders are an even more extreme measure of emptiness: they take up no disk space at all. For proof, create 352,449 folders and get properties on it." I'm guessing this is a joke and I'm just taking it too seriously, but the only thing that "proves" is that Windows lies to you lol. It's obviously information that's stored _somewhere_.

It says the folders are evaluated in alphabetical order, but actually it's evaluating them in natural sort[1][2]. This makes sense since Windows also displays folders in natural sort order. [1] https://github.com/rottytooth/Folders/blob/015cf65c15ab681f5... [2] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_sort_order
This is so nuts and pointless... I love it! The kind of thing no AI would ever come up with :)
I can't decide if I'm in awe, or angry. At least it looks more useful than the flying Tesla.
Imagine being the guy trying to figure out why a Windows server is running out of space, and finding 23 million empty folders being used to define software for prod.

cards.title: Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites: experts

depth.text: Meta’s new **business terms** could let it **scrape news sites** tied to **business accounts**

Starting **October 30**, business accounts that keep using Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp agree to terms letting Meta **crawl associated websites** and use their content to **train its products**. Legal experts say this could reach publishers’ sites; Meta points to robots.txt controls, but there’s no opt-out short of stopping business use, and experts say the terms may override other blocking instructions.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say Meta may not need a site’s consent to scrape, or doubt a court would enforce the terms; others call the move coercive and say businesses may leave Meta.

cards.title: Using AI to reverse engineer hardware

depth.text: someone used **AI** to compare Windows and Linux device traces, then improve **Linux drivers**

Christian Schaller turned his earlier bespoke setup into **hw-harness**: run a vendor Windows driver in a KVM virtual machine, capture **USB traffic** on Linux with usbmon, then compare it with Linux-driver traces. He says AI can read captures and write tests, but he checked every result on the **actual hardware**. In his single-unit, single-frame comparison, his scanner driver took 34.6 s at full resolution versus 54.4 s for upstream.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters see a way to get unsupported devices working; others worry AI makes copying competitors’ algorithms easy.

cards.title: BIPM decides to stop adding leap seconds to UTC

depth.text: the world's timekeepers are stopping **leap seconds**, so computer clocks can keep **running smoothly**

The CGPM says **continuous UTC** takes effect on **20 May 2027**, with the allowed gap between UTC and Earth-rotation time rising to **3 600 seconds (1 hour)**. A 2025 workshop estimated a 30 % chance of a negative leap second by 2035, which the resolution says could disrupt critical infrastructure.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters say ending leap seconds avoids software headaches; critics say it pushes the problem onto future generations.

comments.text: Context: BIPM is responsible for the UTC time standard, and in this document they decide to stop adding (or removing) leap seconds, starting on 20th of May 2027 and lasting for the foreseeable future (until one leap hour is needed, but even then it's unclear if they'll do something). Together with the decision to not add a leap second in December, the 27 leap seconds that have been added so far…

The decision not to add leap seconds was already taken. This resolves the remaining issue (the agreement which brings UTC into existence says it tracks solar time, but TAI doesn't actually do that) by kicking this particular can so far into the bushes that our civilisation almost certainly won't ever need to resolve it, while also acknowledging that if you were annoyed by it thousands of years in…
Solar time never cared about seconds, and leap-seconds were always stupid. Long overdue. Sad they didn't realize this in 1972 and avoid all the silliness in between.
Is this the prelude to dropping UTC altogether?

Goodbye sundial welcome cesium clock. Astrology app devs: remember to carry the drift in Temporal for the Ascendant, specially around 2267 you might get your love and money life predictions messed up.

cards.title: RPKI now protects 70% of internet routes

depth.text: more networks are checking **who can announce internet routes**, and invalid routes barely **travel**

RPKI-valid routed prefixes rose from **54.0% in September 2025 to 70.3% in September 2026**. A typical valid prefix was seen by 596 vantage points, while an invalid one reached **just two**; **China** accounted for almost 60% of the global gain counted by addresses.

The 1991 **Senate Bill 266** resolution was non-binding; if made law, it would have forced manufacturers of secure communications equipment to add **“trap doors”** so the government could read encrypted messages. cards.title: The First Social Network: In rural Argentina residents send messages w AM radio

depth.text: people in rural Argentina use **AM radio** to send **personal messages** across isolated distances

Messages reach stations by **phone, WhatsApp, or scrawled note**, then hosts **read them aloud**. One family heard about a visiting medical team over the radio and got their sick son to a hospital for an **appendectomy**.

comments.text:
The distances and remoteness mentioned in the article are impressive. And is the human need and ingenuity for communication.
It reminded me of William Gibson's description of 1950s farmers in the US using metal wire fences as radio antennas. In the 70s and 80s (and probably before) in the UK, the BBC used to broadcast occasional "sos messages" [1] prior to the main daily news summaries on FM…

Sailing communities have a tradition called "Cruisers' Net", some of them having started back in 1950-60. Usually in the morning via VHF different people will take turns speaking and doing parts. They'll do segments like weather, arrivals/departures, events, buy/sell/trade, etc.

It's interesting to see use-cases like this "in the wild" (as opposed to some hobbyist group trying stuff out). With a little investment, I think Meshtastic/Reticulum could do wonders for communities like this. With Argentina being largely flat, even putting up a relatively short mast on the roof of a house should give it a good enough range (~10-30km).

I'm from the area where this happens (My city is actually named in the article). Can confirm that this is, effectively, a staple of normal life around there. Calling it "the first social network" made me chuckle. Younger generations might not be aware of this mostly due to reduced AM radio audiences, but my daughters (3x ~30 yo) do know what this is about.

glossary.software rendering: A way for the computer’s main chip to draw a game’s picture instead of handing the drawing to a graphics card.
glossary.bilinear filtering: A way to smooth a game’s blocky patterns by blending nearby colors, which can make them look blurry.
glossary.CPU: Central Processing Unit: the main chip that runs instructions in a computer.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.VESA: Video Electronics Standards Association: the group that set common screen rules, including ones used by DOS games to offer higher resolutions.
glossary.anti-aliasing: A way to soften jagged edges in an image so lines look smoother.
glossary.DOSBox: A program that imitates an old DOS computer so DOS games can run on newer machines.
glossary.texel: One tiny square of color in a game’s surface pattern, like a pixel in a picture.
glossary.esolang: An experimental programming language, usually made to explore an idea or for fun rather than everyday use.
glossary.ordered tree: A way to arrange things in branches where the order of items at each level matters.
glossary.imperative language: A language where a program gives the computer steps to carry out.
glossary.interpreter: A program that reads code and carries out what it says.
glossary.natural sort: Sorting names so numbers are treated as numbers, putting “2” before “10.”
glossary.scraping: Using automated tools to collect content from websites.
glossary.robots.txt: A file that tells automated visitors which parts of a website the owner would prefer them not to visit; it cannot force them to obey.
glossary.tying: Making access to one product depend on accepting another condition.
glossary.fair use: A legal rule that can allow some uses of copyrighted work without permission.
glossary.hw-harness: A set of scripts that records what a device does under one driver and compares it with another.
glossary.KVM: Kernel-based Virtual Machine: a Linux feature for running virtual machines.
glossary.usbmon: A Linux tool that records the messages sent over USB.
glossary.driver: Software that lets a computer communicate with a piece of hardware.
glossary.trace: A record of the messages exchanged while a device performs an action.
glossary.UTC: Coordinated Universal Time: a shared time standard that doesn't change with your local clock.
glossary.leap second: A one-second adjustment to official clocks to keep them aligned with Earth's rotation.
glossary.negative leap second: A one-second adjustment that removes a second from UTC instead of adding one.
glossary.TAI: International Atomic Time: a time scale that runs at the same rate as UTC, but differs from it by a whole number of seconds.
glossary.UT1: A time scale based on Earth's rotation.
glossary.CGPM: General Conference on Weights and Measures: the body that makes international decisions about measurement standards.
glossary.BIPM: International Bureau of Weights and Measures: the organization that produces UTC.
glossary.IERS: International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service: an organization that provides information about how Earth's rotation differs from UTC.
glossary.RPKI: Resource Public Key Infrastructure: a system that lets an address holder publish which networks are allowed to announce its addresses.
glossary.BGP: Border Gateway Protocol: the system networks use to tell one another where to send internet traffic.
glossary.ROA: Route Origin Authorization: a signed record listing which networks may announce a block of IP addresses.
glossary.ASPA: Autonomous System Provider Authorization: a signed record listing a network's allowed upstream providers, so others can check the path traffic took.
glossary.prefix: A block of IP addresses that a network announces as a group.
glossary.vantage point: One network's view of which routes are visible.
glossary.HEVC: High Efficiency Video Coding: a way to shrink video so it takes less data to send.
glossary.VPN: Virtual private network: a service that sends your internet traffic through another computer, often to protect it or make it appear to come from somewhere else.
glossary.VNC: Virtual Network Computing: a way to view and control another computer over a network.
glossary.Sidecar: Apple’s feature for using an iPad as another screen for a Mac.
glossary.Direct Wireless Connection: A direct wireless link lets the Mac and device connect without sharing a network.
glossary.PGP: Pretty Good Privacy: a tool for protecting messages and checking that they came from the person who sent them.
glossary.cryptography: Ways of protecting information by turning it into a form other people can't read.
glossary.trap doors: Hidden ways built into a communication product that let someone bypass its normal protection.
glossary.plain text: Data sent without protection that would stop someone watching the connection from reading it.
glossary.key exchange: The step where people share what is needed to encrypt and decrypt messages.
glossary.Sokoban: A puzzle style where you push boxes or other objects around a board.
glossary.overworld: The large map that connects different areas of a game.
glossary.eureka moment: The sudden moment when a puzzle’s solution clicks.
glossary.native service: A program that runs directly on the server, rather than inside a separate container.
glossary.container: A way to run a program in a separated space, limiting what it can access.
glossary.Podman: A tool for starting and managing containers on a computer.
glossary.systemd: A Linux tool that starts programs in the background and keeps track of them.
glossary.cold-gas thrusters: Small engines that push a vehicle by releasing gas without burning fuel.
glossary.active aero: Moving parts on a car that change how air flows around it.
glossary.downforce: A force that pushes a car toward the road so its tires can grip.
glossary.COPV: Composite Overwrapped Pressure Vessel: a reinforced tank built to hold gas at high pressure.
glossary.ITAR: International Traffic in Arms Regulations: US rules that restrict sharing certain military-related technology.
glossary.dual use: Technology that can be used for both civilian and military purposes.
glossary.malware: Software made to harm a computer or get access to it without permission.
glossary.executable: A file that runs as a program when opened.
glossary.Sonarr: A tool that searches for and organizes TV episodes you want.
glossary.Radarr: A tool like Sonarr, but for managing movie downloads.
glossary.qBittorrent: A program for downloading files shared through torrents.
glossary.blocklist: A list of files or sources a tool should reject or remove.
glossary.public tracker: A public service that helps people find torrent downloads.
glossary.torrent: A way of sharing files by downloading pieces from other people's computers.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.HealthKit: Apple’s system for letting apps share health information with Apple Health.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.reverse-engineering: Figuring out how a device or program works by examining it, rather than relying on its instructions.
glossary.Bluetooth: A wireless way for nearby devices, like a phone and watch, to connect.
glossary.GLP-1: Glucagon-like peptide-1: a body chemical involved in appetite and blood sugar; medicines that act on it can change how hungry someone feels.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first offers its shares for the public to buy.
glossary.Lean certificate: A proof written in a format a computer can check step by step.
glossary.formal verification: Checking a claim using precise rules, often with a computer.
glossary.CAS: Computer Algebra System: software that can simplify and solve math expressions such as x² + 2x.
glossary.vibecoding: Using AI to make software from requests instead of writing each line yourself.
glossary.Library of Babel: A thought experiment about a library containing every possible book, including books that make no sense.
glossary.AM radio: Amplitude modulation: a way of sending sound over radio waves.
glossary.Mensajero Rural: Spanish for “Rural Messenger”; it’s the radio program that reads messages for people in remote areas.
glossary.Meshtastic: A tool for sending messages between small radios without relying on cell service.
glossary.VHF: Very high frequency: radio waves used for short-range communication, including boat radios.
glossary.white reflectivity: How much light a screen reflects when it shows white.
glossary.front light: A light that shines across the front of an e-reader screen so you can see it in dim conditions.
glossary.subpixels: Tiny colored parts of a screen that combine to make the colors you see.
glossary.RGB: Red, green, blue: the colors a screen combines to show many other colors.
glossary.electrophoresis: A way to move charged particles using electricity; in e-paper, this can move pigment around to change what the screen shows.
glossary.optical coherence tomography: A way to make detailed images of layers inside something without cutting it open.
glossary.PCB: Printed Circuit Board: a flat board that holds electronic parts and connects them with metal paths.
